title: Natural Language Query Engine for Relational Databases using Generative AI
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of making relational databases accessible to non-technical users who do not know SQL. It argues that existing natural-language-to-SQL solutions often fail to ensure syntactic correctness, semantic correctness, or faithful handling of domain-specific business rules, and that they also typically leave users with raw SQL or poorly explained outputs.

The proposed approach is a generative-AI-based natural language assistant for querying relational databases. The system scans database structure, vectorizes schema metadata and business rules, stores them in a vector database, and retrieves relevant context for a user query. It then uses large language models to generate SQL, validate it syntactically and semantically, iteratively refine errors, and finally produce a well-formed natural-language response from the retrieved data. The prototype is implemented with IBM watsonx.data, watsonx.ai, Milvus, Python, and a Streamlit frontend.

The paper reports an initial prototype evaluation on the BIRD-SQL benchmark, which consists of database-grounded text-to-SQL queries. Results are presented as early prototype performance rather than a controlled educational study: over 50% of queries were correctly translated on the first attempt, with better performance on simpler queries, and the author reports that nontechnical users rated generated natural-language responses as highly understandable. Overall, the paper concludes that generative AI plus vector retrieval can support more accurate and user-friendly database querying, though it still faces challenges with ambiguous queries, specialized business rules, execution time, and scalability.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical preprint/prototype paper with an initial benchmark evaluation, not a peer-reviewed education study or a well-designed causal design in K-12 settings. It lacks randomized or quasi-experimental evidence and does not test the educational comparisons in the retrieval topic.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate K-12 learning outcomes or any student-facing educational impact. Any claimed benefits are limited to database-query usability and productivity in an enterprise prototype, so there is no evidentiary basis for educational impact in the requested domain.

interventions.use_case: Natural-language querying assistant for relational databases that uses LLMs to translate user questions into SQL, validate queries, and generate natural-language responses from retrieved data.
Vector-database-backed retrieval of database schema metadata and business rules to support semantic query generation and validation for natural-language database access.

finding.finding_summary: The prototype is presented as improving user productivity and reducing the need for SQL expertise by allowing non-technical users to query databases directly in natural language. In the reported BIRD-SQL evaluation, over 50% of queries were translated correctly on the first attempt and more than 58% for simple queries, with iterative refinement improving success further; the paper also reports that 90% of responses were rated excellent by a dozen nontechnical users. These results are framed as evidence of improved efficiency, though no formal workload effect size is reported.
finding.measure: SQL translation accuracy; natural-language response quality ratings; user productivity/accessibility claims

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues the system democratizes access to relational data for non-expert users by removing the need for SQL knowledge and by incorporating business rules into query generation. This is supported by prototype evaluation on BIRD-SQL and usability feedback from nontechnical users, but the paper does not report institutional outcome measures or causal effects beyond prototype performance.
finding.measure: Access/democratization claims; benchmark performance; user acceptability feedback
